拉夫塔琴以撥片撥弦發聲，右手技巧與烏德相近，使用長而薄的撥片。初學可先熟悉四組七: The lavta sounds when a plectrum strikes the strings; the right-hand technique is close to the oud's and uses a long, thin plectrum. Beginners can first learn the layout and tuning of the four courses of seven strings, then practise striking the strings steadily with the plectrum; the basic order is to check the tuning first and then to pluck.
拉夫塔琴源自伊斯坦堡，亞美尼亞語稱lavuta，希臘語稱Politiko lao: The lavta comes from Istanbul; in Armenian it is called lavuta, in Greek Politiko laouto or lafta. It was popular from the late nineteenth to the early twentieth century, especially in Greek and Armenian communities, and was also played by Tanburi Cemil Bey. In the early twentieth century it took on the microtones of the makam system; before that it was diatonic. It was gradually displaced by the oud but survived; since the 1980s there has been a revival, and today it is found mainly in Greece and Turkey.
拉夫塔琴為撥弦樂器，以腸弦發聲，七弦四組，可調品以尼龍綁於指板，早期用腸線。其音: The lavta is a plucked instrument sounding from gut strings, seven strings in four courses; the movable frets are nylon tied round the fingerboard, and gut was used earlier. Its pitch was diatonic at first, and in the early twentieth century it took on the microtones of the makam system. The right hand plucks with a long, thin plectrum, in a technique close to the oud's. Beside the fretless oud and the diatonic-fretted laouto it stands closer to the tanbur.

The strings are gut, and the movable frets are tied with nylon, historically with gut. The bridge often ends in a peacock shape, the pegbox tilts back, and the pegs are shaped like violin pegs. The famous musician and composer Tanburi Cemil Bey played the instrument, and he is an important reference for the early sound. The right hand plays with a long, thin plectrum, close to the way the oud sounds. Although the oud later displaced it, a revival began in the 1980s in Greece and Turkey, so modern demonstrations are mostly in local traditional music, community playing and revival settings.

The lavta is a plucked instrument of Istanbul, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-5. The body is small and built from many ribs joined by bending, so it looks like a small Turkish oud; seven gut strings are grouped in four courses, and the fingerboard carries movable nylon frets. It was diatonic at first, and in the early twentieth century it took on the microtones of the makam system. The right hand holds a slender plectrum, much as on the oud. From the late nineteenth to the early twentieth century it was popular in Greek and Armenian communities, and it was one of the instruments played by Tanburi Cemil Bey.
